before: Every personal injury claim in the United States is subject to a statute of limitations — a legal deadline that determines how long you have to file a lawsuit after suffering an injury. In Georgia and South Carolina, these deadlines vary depending on the type of case, who caused the injury, and when the injury was discovered. Missing the deadline almost always means losing your right to compensation entirely, regardless of how strong your case may be. Understanding these timelines is one of the most important steps you can take after an accident. For more information about how statutes of limitations work in personal injury law, the Cornell Law Institute provides a comprehensive overview of limitation periods across legal contexts.

Missing the deadline almost always means losing your right to compensation entirely, regardless of how strong your case may be. Understanding these timelines is one of the most important steps you can take after an accident. For more information about how statutes of limitations work in personal injury law, the Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute provides a concise overview of limitation periods across legal contexts.

before: If the injured person is a minor at the time of the accident, the statute of limitations is generally tolled until they reach the age of 18. In Georgia, minors then have two years from their 18th birthday to file. In South Carolina, the three-year clock begins at age 18.
after: If the injured person is a minor at the time of the accident, the statute of limitations is generally tolled until they reach the age of 18. In Georgia, minors then have two years from their 18th birthday to file (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-90; medical malpractice runs on a shorter clock under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-73). In South Carolina, the extension ends one year after the child turns 18, so the deadline is the 19th birthday, or three years from the injury if that is later (S.C. Code § 15-3-40).

before: If the injured person is mentally incapacitated at the time of the injury, the statute may be tolled for the duration of the incapacity. This can apply to victims who suffer traumatic brain injuries that prevent them from understanding their legal rights.
after: If the injured person is mentally incapacitated at the time of the injury, the statute may be tolled. In Georgia the clock waits until the incapacity is removed (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-90); South Carolina caps the extension at five years, and at one year after the incapacity ends (S.C. Code § 15-3-40). This can apply to victims who suffer traumatic brain injuries that prevent them from understanding their legal rights.

before: In Georgia, under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-94, if the defendant leaves the state after causing the injury, the time spent outside Georgia does not count toward the statute of limitations. South Carolina has a similar tolling provision for absent defendants.
after: Georgia's tolling statute for defendants who move away (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-94) rarely helps in an accident case: courts apply it only when the move actually makes the defendant impossible to serve, and an out-of-state driver can still be served under Georgia's long-arm statute. South Carolina's version (S.C. Code § 15-3-30) applies only when the defendant resides out of state or stays away a year or more. Do not count on either.

before: If the defendant actively conceals the cause of injury or commits fraud to prevent the plaintiff from discovering the claim, courts may toll the deadline in both states.
after: If the defendant actively conceals the cause of injury or commits fraud to prevent the plaintiff from discovering the claim, the deadline can be extended in both states: in Georgia by statute (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-96), in South Carolina through the discovery rule (S.C. Code § 15-3-535).

before:
In most accident cases, the statute of limitations clock starts on the date of the injury. However, both Georgia and South Carolina recognize the discovery rule in certain situations — particularly medical malpractice and toxic exposure cases — where the injury may not be immediately apparent.

Under the discovery rule, the statute of limitations begins when the injured person knew or reasonably should have known about the injury and its potential cause. For example, if a surgeon leaves a foreign object inside a patient, the clock may not start until the patient discovers or reasonably should have discovered the object, even if the surgery occurred years earlier.

However, both states impose statutes of repose that set an absolute outer limit. In Georgia, the medical malpractice statute of repose is five years under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71. In South Carolina, it is six years under S.C. Code § 15-3-545. These hard deadlines cannot be extended by the discovery rule.
after:
In most accident cases, the statute of limitations clock starts on the date of the injury. South Carolina has a true discovery rule: for any personal injury claim, the three years run from when you knew or reasonably should have known you had a claim (S.C. Code § 15-3-535), including medical malpractice (S.C. Code § 15-3-545). Georgia does not. Its two-year clock runs from the injury, in medical malpractice cases too, whether or not you knew about it (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71). Georgia's discovery-type exceptions are narrow: a foreign object left in the body, fraud by the defendant, and ongoing exposure treated as a continuing tort.

Under South Carolina's discovery rule, the statute of limitations begins when the injured person knew or reasonably should have known about the injury and its potential cause. Both states also have a special rule for foreign objects: if a surgeon leaves one inside a patient, the clock may not start until the patient discovers or reasonably should have discovered the object, even if the surgery occurred years earlier — one year from discovery in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-72), two years from discovery in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-545(B)).

However, both states impose statutes of repose that set an absolute outer limit. In Georgia, the medical malpractice statute of repose is five years under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71. In South Carolina, it is six years under S.C. Code § 15-3-545. These hard deadlines cannot be extended by late discovery or, in Georgia, by fraud — the foreign-object statutes above are the one exception.

before: Workers' compensation claims operate under their own separate deadlines. In Georgia, injured workers must report the injury to their employer within 30 days and file a claim with the State Board of Workers' Compensation within one year of the injury under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82. In South Carolina, the deadline to file is two years from the injury under S.C. Code § 42-15-40.
after: Workers' compensation claims operate under their own separate deadlines. In Georgia, injured workers must report the injury to their employer within 30 days (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80) and file a claim with the State Board of Workers' Compensation within one year of the injury under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82. In South Carolina, notice to the employer is due within 90 days (S.C. Code § 42-15-20), and the deadline to file is two years from the injury under S.C. Code § 42-15-40.

before: Product liability claims in Georgia follow the standard two-year personal injury deadline but are subject to a 10-year statute of repose under O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11 from the date the product was first sold. South Carolina applies the three-year limitation with its own product liability repose provisions.
after: Product liability claims in Georgia follow the standard two-year personal injury deadline but are subject to a 10-year statute of repose under O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11 from the date the product was first sold. South Carolina applies the three-year limitation, running from when the injury was or should have been discovered (S.C. Code § 15-3-535), and has no product liability statute of repose.

before: Maritime injury claims and boating accident cases may fall under federal maritime law, which imposes a three-year statute of limitations regardless of the state. Jones Act claims for injured seamen also carry a three-year deadline.
after: Maritime injury claims and boating accident cases may fall under federal maritime law, which imposes a three-year statute of limitations regardless of the state (46 U.S.C. § 30106). Jones Act claims for injured seamen also carry a three-year deadline (46 U.S.C. § 30104; 45 U.S.C. § 56).

before: Under O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5, claims against Georgia municipalities require an ante-litem notice within six months of the incident. Claims against the state itself require notice under O.C.G.A. § 50-21-26 within 12 months. Failing to provide this notice within the required timeframe bars the claim entirely, even if the general statute of limitations has not expired.
after: Under O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5, claims against Georgia municipalities require an ante-litem notice within six months of the incident. Claims against a county (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1) and against the state itself (O.C.G.A. § 50-21-26) require notice within 12 months. Failing to provide this notice within the required timeframe bars the claim entirely, even if the general statute of limitations has not expired.

before: Under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act, claims against government entities must be filed within two years of the incident (S.C. Code § 15-78-110). South Carolina requires no pre-suit notice: filing a verified claim with the agency within one year is optional, and doing so extends the deadline to three years (S.C. Code § 15-78-80). There are also caps on the amount of damages recoverable against government defendants in South Carolina.
after: Under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act, claims against government entities must be filed within two years of the incident (S.C. Code § 15-78-110). South Carolina requires no pre-suit notice: filing a verified claim with the agency within one year is optional, and doing so extends the deadline to three years (S.C. Code § 15-78-80). Damages against government defendants in South Carolina are also capped at $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence (S.C. Code § 15-78-120).

before: In rare circumstances, courts may apply equitable tolling if the plaintiff can demonstrate extraordinary circumstances that prevented timely filing. However, these exceptions are narrow and difficult to prove. The safest course of action is always to file well before the deadline.
after: In rare circumstances, South Carolina courts have applied equitable tolling where extraordinary circumstances prevented timely filing (Hooper v. Ebenezer Senior Services, 2009); Georgia's exceptions are the statutory tolling rules above. Either way, these exceptions are narrow and difficult to prove. The safest course of action is always to file well before the deadline.

before: Georgia allows two years to file personal injury lawsuits under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33, while South Carolina allows three years under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. Exceptions include tolling for minors, mental incapacity, and the discovery rule. Government claims run on shorter clocks — ante litem notice within six months for a Georgia city, and a two-year filing deadline under South Carolina's Tort Claims Act. Missing the deadline permanently bars recovery.
after: Georgia allows two years to file personal injury lawsuits under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33, while South Carolina allows three years under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. Government claims run on shorter clocks — ante litem notice within six months for a Georgia city, and a two-year filing deadline under South Carolina's Tort Claims Act. Missing the deadline permanently bars recovery.

before: Georgia has a two-year statute of limitations for most personal injury claims under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. The clock generally starts on the date of the injury, though exceptions like the discovery rule may apply in certain cases.
